blocks.prompt: The Caterpillar That Turned to Soup
blocks.text: A butterfly does not start out as a butterfly. It starts as an egg on a leaf. A tiny caterpillar hatches out. The caterpillar eats and eats. It grows so fast that its skin gets too tight, so it wriggles out of it. Then it hangs upside down and makes a hard shell called a chrysalis. Inside the shell, its whole body changes. Wings grow. Legs grow. A long drinking tube grows. One day the shell splits open and a butterfly climbs out. It waits for its wet wings to dry. Then it flies away to find a flower.

blocks.prompt: Four Lives in One
blocks.text: A butterfly lives four different lives, and it looks different in every one. It begins as an egg, smaller than a grain of rice, glued to the underside of a leaf. Out of the egg crawls a caterpillar, and a caterpillar has one job: eat. It chews leaves all day and grows so quickly that its skin cannot keep up. Five times or so, the caterpillar splits its old skin and crawls out wearing a new one. Then the eating stops. The caterpillar finds a safe twig, hangs upside down, and sheds its skin one last time. Underneath is not a caterpillar at all. It is a chrysalis, a smooth hard case. This is not a cocoon. Moths spin cocoons out of silk. A chrysalis is the animal's own skin, gone hard. Inside the case, the caterpillar comes apart. Most of its body turns to mush, and out of that mush a butterfly is built. Two weeks later the case splits and the butterfly pulls itself out with crumpled, wet wings. It pumps fluid into them, waits for them to dry, and flies off to look for nectar.

blocks.prompt: The Body That Rebuilds Itself
blocks.text: Every butterfly you have ever seen used to be a chewing machine with no wings. That is the strange part of complete metamorphosis. A caterpillar and a butterfly are the same animal, but they share almost nothing. The caterpillar has stubby legs, simple eyes, and jaws built for shredding leaves. The butterfly has four scaled wings, compound eyes, and no jaws at all. Instead it drinks through a proboscis, a coiled tube that works like a straw and rolls up under its head when it is not being used. The changeover happens inside the chrysalis. Most people picture a caterpillar quietly sprouting wings in there. What actually happens is closer to demolition. The caterpillar releases enzymes that break down most of its own tissue, and the inside of the chrysalis becomes a thick soup. Floating in that soup are small clusters of cells called imaginal discs. The caterpillar was born with them and carried them, unused, its whole life. Each disc holds the plan for one adult part: a wing, an eye, a leg. Fed by the soup of its old body, each disc grows into the part it was always going to be. Not everything dissolves. The heart keeps beating. Parts of the nervous system carry through, which is why a butterfly is not simply a new animal in a used container. About two weeks later, the case cracks. The butterfly hauls itself out with wings like wet crumpled paper, then pumps hemolymph, the insect version of blood, into the wing veins until they stiffen and flatten. An hour or two later it can fly. It has traded a life of eating for a life of finding flowers, and it will never chew anything again.

blocks.prompt: The Butterfly With a Map It Was Never Given
blocks.text: In late summer, in a backyard somewhere in Ontario or Minnesota, a monarch butterfly comes out of its chrysalis and does something none of its parents did. It turns south, and it keeps going. The monarchs that hatch earlier in the summer live about two to six weeks. They mate, lay eggs on milkweed, and die. The generation that emerges in late summer is different. Shorter days and cooler nights switch off its urge to breed and switch on an urge to travel. This generation lives eight or nine months, and it flies as far as three thousand miles, down through the United States and into a handful of mountaintop forests in central Mexico. There it clusters on oyamel fir trees in numbers so dense the branches sag, and it waits out the winter. Here is the part that keeps biologists busy. Not one of those butterflies has been there before. Their great-grandparents made the trip. The route is not learned, and it cannot be taught, because every butterfly that knew it is dead. Whatever guides them is built in. Part of the answer sits in their antennae. Monarchs steer by the sun, but the sun moves across the sky all day, so a fixed sun-heading would send them in a curve. To correct for that, they run a clock. Researchers found that the timing clock is not only in the brain but in the antennae themselves. Remove the antennae, and a monarch loses its bearings. There is also evidence they can sense Earth's magnetic field, which would help on overcast days. Their food supply defends them. Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, a plant loaded with poisons called cardenolides that attack the heart. The caterpillar stores the poison instead of breaking it down, and carries it into adulthood. A bird that eats a monarch usually vomits, and it remembers those orange wings. People did not know where the monarchs went until 1975, when a search organized by Fred and Norah Urquhart finally found the Mexican colonies. Fewer than fifty years later, the eastern monarch population has fallen sharply, mostly because the milkweed that feeds it has been cleared from farmland along the route. A butterfly that can navigate a continent cannot do much about a missing plant.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Holometabolous: egg, larva, pupa, adult
Imaginal discs are carried from hatching
Histolysis: larval tissue digested by its own enzymes
The heart keeps beating inside the chrysalis
Manduca sexta moths kept larval learning (2008)
A chrysalis is hardened skin, not spun silk

blocks.prompt: What Survives the Soup
blocks.text: Consider what a caterpillar actually does when it stops eating. It has spent every waking hour of its short life shredding leaves and swelling. Now it walks away from its food, finds a twig, spins a small silk pad, and hangs from it head down. Its skin splits one final time, and what emerges is not another caterpillar. It is a chrysalis: a hard case that is not built around the animal but is the animal, its own outermost layer hardened into a shell. This is the first thing most people have wrong. A cocoon is a blanket a moth spins for itself out of silk. A chrysalis is skin. The second thing most people have wrong is what happens next. The comfortable image is of a caterpillar slowly sprouting wings, growing gradually into its adult shape. The reality is more violent. The insect floods itself with enzymes and digests most of its own body. Muscle, gut, and fat break down into a nutrient-rich broth. If you opened a chrysalis at the right moment, much of what poured out would be liquid. But a soup cannot organize itself into a butterfly, and this is where the trick reveals itself. The caterpillar was never only a caterpillar. From the moment it hatched, it carried small pockets of cells called imaginal discs, folded away and doing nothing. Each disc is a blueprint for one adult structure: a forewing, a hindwing, an antenna, a leg, an eye. They ride along, unused and unnoticed, through every molt. When the demolition begins, they are the only things not demolished. They feed on the broth of the old body and unfold into the new one. The caterpillar is not so much transformed as consumed, and the butterfly is built from the proceeds. Some structures refuse to dissolve at all. The heart keeps beating throughout. The nervous system is heavily remodeled but never destroyed, and that detail turns out to matter. In 2008, researchers at Georgetown trained tobacco hornworm caterpillars, which become moths rather than butterflies, to avoid a particular smell by pairing it with a mild electric shock. The caterpillars pupated. They dissolved. They rebuilt themselves into adult moths. And the moths still avoided the smell. Something the animal learned as a leaf-chewing larva survived the liquefaction of the body that learned it. Why would evolution build anything so extravagant? The usual answer is that it lets one species live two lives without competing with itself. A caterpillar and a butterfly want nothing in common. The larva wants leaves and does not need to travel; the adult wants nectar and needs to travel widely to breed and to spread eggs across many plants. An animal that had to be good at both jobs at once would be mediocre at both. Complete metamorphosis lets the insect specialize completely, twice, and pay for it with a few weeks of helplessness in a case. Roughly four out of five insect species develop this way, and insects account for most of the animal species on Earth, which suggests the bargain is a good one. There is a temptation to make this into a tidy lesson about change and rebirth. It is worth resisting. Nothing about the chrysalis is gentle, and nothing in it is destroyed and replaced by magic. The butterfly is not a reward the caterpillar earns. It is the same animal, carrying the plans for its second body from the day it hatched, and spending the first body to build it.
